chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who performed dhahr (expiation of zihar) with his wife three times. He said: 'He must expiate three times.' I said: 'What if he had intercourse before he expiates?' He said: 'He seeks forgiveness of Allah and holds back until he expiates.' This does not contradict the earlier reports, because in His statement 'so let him hold back until he expiates,' it is not specified that it is the expiation of one or two [times]. And if that is not explicit in its apparent meaning, it is permissible that the intended meaning is not [merely] until he expiates the two expiations.

key_terms.ظَاهَرَ: Zihar (a pre-Islamic form of divorce where a husband compares his wife to his mother's back, requiring expiation)
key_terms.يُكَفِّرُ: He expiates (performs the required ritual expiation)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a man performs zihar multiple times and has intercourse before completing the expiations?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Istibsar* clarifies the cumulative nature of *Kaffarah* (expiation) in *Dharr* (zihar), establishing that each instance requires a separate expiation. The scholar highlights that the Quranic command to 'hold back until he expiates' is interpreted broadly to accommodate multiple expiations rather than limiting it to one or two, thereby resolving apparent textual ambiguities. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle of strict adherence to the literal and contextual implications of Quranic verses in family law.
